title: UNH Students Speak Amid Lawsuit Challenging Restriction of Using Student IDs to Vote - InDepthNH.org
content:
InDepthNH.org (https://indepthnh.org/2026/10/19/unh-students-speak-amid-lawsuit-challenging-restriction-of-using-student-ids-to-vote/) DURHAM — Some students at University of New Hampshire are speaking out in the wake of a lawsuit that challenges the use of student IDs to vote, expressing concerns that it would cause confusion among young voters and limit their ability to participate in politics. House Bill 323 — which made student IDs a no longer valid form of identification to obtain a ballot — was signed into law by Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte in April. That same month, Secretary of State David Scanlan released a directive advising that student IDs cannot be used as proof of ID when registering to vote, requesting an absentee ballot, or checking in to vote in an election. A lawsuit was filed in August by Free Speech for People, representing Coalition for Open Democracy (a voter education and outreach group) asking the Court to enjoin both HB 323 and Scanlan’s directive before the election. “I believe that student IDs are valid in the court system, and because a student ID is just enough of identification like a real ID would be. I don’t know why you need to bring extra identification… I feel like college students don’t really bring — or have other forms of identification, especially since they have a home, but they’re not there very often — so, they keep all of their identification at home. So, it takes a toll on how many people are able to vote,” UNH student Dalaney Trudeau said Monday. Secretary of State Scanlan’s motion for a stay on the legal proceedings for the lawsuit was denied by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, though an emergency stay has been requested from the U.S. Supreme Court. Previously, a federal judge ruled that student IDs can still be considered by election officials at polling places as evidence of voter identity. They can still be used for considering voter identification if supplemented with other documentation. Head of UNH’s Media Relations Tania DeLuzuriaga said the university has not taken a position on the lawsuit. Michael Garrity, spokesman for the New Hampshire Office of the Attorney General, said there were no updates to the case as of Monday. “The State has asked the United States Supreme Court for an emergency stay in this matter. New Hampshire has a strong interest in ensuring that its election laws are applied consistently and that local election officials have clear, workable guidance in administering elections,” Garrity said. Prime sponsor of HB 323, Rep. Donald McFarlane, R-Orange, did not respond for comment. Co-sponsor Rep. Ross Berry, R-Weare, insisted that the public supports the measure. When asked about the concerns from UNH students that the situation would cause confusion among young voters and how they feel it could limit the amounts of students who vote, Berry said: “I don’t see how that is a thing.” Another student, Olivia Rose of Barrington, said it’s unacceptable and restricting their ability to vote doesn’t seem appropriate. She said it would make students more detached from politics because they won’t feel the need to look into what’s going on politically (and) that limiting their ability to vote and participate in politics would make them less likely to try. UNH student Kai Shanahan said being able to use student IDs is a good way to prove voter identification “because sometimes, students aren’t able to get a driver’s license or a non-driver’s ID. Especially since for a lot of people at college, it’s their first time being out of the house.” Shanahan added she feels it would cause more confusion for young voters in college and “definitely stop people from voting.” According to data from July by the Civics Center — a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization aimed at encouraging young people to vote — noted that just 7% of 18-year-olds are registered to vote in the state as of March 31. It also highlighted how “there is not a single county in the state where the rate was at 10% or more as of March.” The data shows that, per county, the various rates of 18-year-olds registered to vote are: Student James Frady, from Massachusetts, said he wasn’t aware of the lawsuit but if a student ID is supplemented with other forms of documentation to prove voter identification that “I see it as a valid marker that you’re here at UNH and you’re in the system.” “I’m from Massachusetts, and I voted in Massachusetts, but I think it’s definitely a hassle to get all the documents in order. And that could definitely make it easier if student IDs were allowed as an option,” Frady said. House Democratic Leader Rep. Alexis Simpson, D-Exeter said: “Eligible voters have a fundamental right to cast a ballot, and deliberately removing ways to prove identity is voter suppression. For six years, Republicans have made it harder to register, vote absentee, and prove identity at the polls as the cost of living has skyrocketed. If Republicans had an agenda Granite Staters wanted, they would run on that instead of attacking the right to vote.” House Majority Leader Jason Osborne, R-Auburn said he did not have any comments on the matter. title: University of New Haven student killed by wrong-way driver remembered as campus leader - WFSB
content:
NEW HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - Ryan O’Shea, a University of New Haven student described as a club hockey captain, fraternity president and campus leader, was killed by a wrong-way driver in North Haven on Friday night. O’Shea, 21, was set to graduate in the spring. He had interned with the NYPD and wanted to become a police officer with the department after graduation. O’Shea was the assistant captain of UNH’s club hockey team. The team had a game Friday night, and O’Shea was driving back to campus afterward. He was on Route 91 South in North Haven just before midnight when state police say 31-year-old Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, of Bridgeport, was driving the wrong way and crashed into O’Shea head-on. O’Shea was then hit by two other drivers and died. Carmona-Lopez is in the hospital fighting for his life. He has not been charged, and state police are still investigating. Ophelie Rowe-Allen, vice president of student affairs at UNH, said O’Shea represented the university well. “Our students are always looking for opportunities on campus to be leaders, good citizens, good stewardesses and to represent the university at all times and that’s what Ryan was doing for us,” Rowe-Allen said. “That was very hard to hear and to know Ryan was coming from a hockey game with his teammates, was very excited and ready for the next game the following day,” Rowe-Allen said. “It’s a very, very sad time for us,” Rowe-Allen said. In a statement, O’Shea’s teammates wrote: “Ryan embodied what it meant to be a Charger. His infectious personality and sense of humor lit up our locker room.” Jackson Brentson, a UNH senior, said O’Shea had an impact on those around him. “I know people who knew him and it seems he had an impact on people and people cared about him and it’s just really awful that something like were to happen,” Brentson said. “I hope the family has a lot of support right now. It’s unimaginable, just awful,” Brentson said. School officials have been in touch with O’Shea’s family. His funeral is set for Friday. The university is setting up travel accommodations for students and offering counseling. O’Shea was from Stony Point, New York, about 40 miles north of Manhattan. O’Shea’s death is the second wrong-way crash death in Connecticut this year. There has been a significant drop in those deaths in recent years: 23 in 2022, 13 in 2024, and seven last year. The Connecticut Department of Transportation has installed 300 wrong-way detection systems on highway on-ramps around the state. The systems have gone off 1,300 times, and in 1,100 of those cases, drivers self-corrected before getting onto the highway. title: What Do History Majors Do? - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you fascinated with how things used to be and what that means for us now? History is the study of the past and how that knowledge can inform the present and the future. This is a broad degree program, allowing you to focus on a particular country, region, time period, or aspect of human culture that interests you, such as religion, science, or cultural movements. You’ll develop the skills in critical reading and writing that form the basis of a solid liberal arts education and prepare you for a wide range of careers, as well as graduate or professional school. Meet William Kirkpatrick '26, a history major from Eliot, Maine, who has found a close community on the UNH campus, with plenty of room to explore by studying how dinosaur bones may have influenced Greek mythology and by studying abroad in Turkey. William Kirkpatrick: I chose UNH because the campus has the appeal of the beautiful small schools of New England while providing enough opportunities, classes, and people to feel like a significant step up from my small Maine high school. Growing up with two parents who worked at UNH, I also had the opportunity to meet some of the professors, faculty, and staff, all of whom were extremely kind and welcoming. It seemed like an easy choice. My favorite thing about COLA is that almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before. Coming in my first year, I certainly didn't think I would write a final paper two years later comparing Odysseus in Homer's "The Odyssey" to Mad Max. I can't think of another college that would actively encourage such ambitions. "Almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before." I love the history department because of the many subjects it offers. One class will have me writing about medieval hunting practices, and the next will provide the opportunity to present about why dinosaur bones have heavily influenced Greek mythology. I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner after considering the presented material. Paraphrasing Professor Gregory McMahon, a liberal arts education is a lesson in persuasion, critical thinking, and independence presented in the most fascinating way possible. I agree! "I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner." My most impactful professors are both Professor Gregory McMahon and Professor David Bachrach. During my first semester freshman year, Professor Bachrach taught me how to write like a historian and encouraged me to reach out to him with drafts of all my papers. I still refer to some of my papers from that year for format and grammar. Then, in my sophomore year, Professor McMahon helped me understand how fun it is to create new ideas based on ancient sources and supported me when I would come to him with frankly crazy ideas for papers. Professor McMahon sent me to study abroad on his archaeological dig in Turkey this summer. I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life. It's such a vastly different culture from ours, but I fit right in since everyone I met treated me as if they had known me their whole life. In addition to the amazing Turkish culture, getting to see, touch, and excavate the artifacts that I've spent so much of my college career reading about, analyzing, and writing about is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I can hopefully turn into a twice-in-a-lifetime experience in the near future. "I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life." I received the Trustee's Scholarship coming in my freshman year. This scholarship allowed me to free up money to study abroad in Turkey this summer. I will be forever grateful that UNH allowed me the opportunity to experience Turkish culture from a perspective that many people are not afforded. There are two pieces of advice I would give my freshman self. The first is to explore the campus earlier. There are many cool areas, such as College Woods, the Fishbowl, and the tennis courts, that I never really used until later on. UNH is meant to be explored, and everyone has their favorite spot on campus to study and hang out. The second piece is to study abroad earlier. If I had the chance to go on a second trip before graduation, I would have taken it immediately. I was originally scared that I would feel alone, homesick, and out of place, but I found the opposite was true. There will never be another opportunity to experience international culture like that offered in college, so why not take it? I have found a sense of community within my friend group. Most of us met during the "Become the Roar" tradition during orientation, and we have stayed very close friends throughout all four years. My freshman year roommate is still my best friend, and all of us shared an eight-person suite in Mills Hall during my sophomore year. One thing people might be surprised to learn about me is that during the summers, I work as a groundskeeper for my local cemetery. After someone learns this, I am immediately asked if I bury the people, too, which, yes, I do. However, I am hopefully far from the cemetery groundskeeper stereotype. title: Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks - CNBC
content:
Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times. Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential. Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street’s top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan. Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. “UNH’s beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher ’26 EPS baseline & upside to ’27 consensus,” said Wright. The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company’s 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. Furthermore, Wright highlighted management’s view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company’s 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17. Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH’s operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution. Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks. Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company’s AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21. Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call. Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse’s current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta’s 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization. “Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta’s core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets,” said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework. While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company’s strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base. Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks. Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds. After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell’s senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370. The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell’s Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60. While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell’s XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business. Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell’s supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts. Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. title: Run game paves way for Monmouth's dominant first-ever win over UNH - Asbury Park Press
content: It's one thing to break down a longstanding barrier, it's another bulldoze right through it. Monmouth football did the latter on Saturday afternoon in Durham, N.H. For four straight years, the Hawks had lost to New Hampshire since joining the Coastal Athletic Association in 2022. They made sure that the fifth opportunity would erase any lingering memories of those past disappointments. Monmouth went on the road and dominated the Wildcats for four quarters, getting their first-ever victory over New Hampshire in a 42-21 rout to improve to 5-2 and remain unbeaten in conference play. "On the road, winning a CAA game is huge," Monmouth head coach Jeff Gallo said. "It's about this team, this year, and our opportunity to come get this game and make a point. It's for our former players who played these games and lost some tough ones to them. And I felt good going into it. We fought all the way through. We started fast, we out-physicaled them, and we took control of the game." The final score would be enough of a testament to the team's dominant effort, but the manner in which the win unfolded further reflected the emphatic showing by the Hawks. FCS No. 20 Monmouth ran the ball 62 times for 326 yards and four touchdowns. Both Kenny Smith Jr. (175) and Elijah Jennings (126) surpassed the century mark on the day on what was easily the team's most prolific ground performance of the season. The Hawks raced out of the gates and never looked back. After forcing a three-and-out, Monmouth ran the ball with Jennings on the first six plays of the game before the seventh was a 2-yard touchdown run by former Keyport standout Nazir Treadwell, who added 22 more rushing yards to the impressive total. After another UNH three-and-out, the Hawks' second drive of the game was the start of a career day for Smith, as five of the seven plays were runs to the redshirt freshman including the 6-yard touchdown to finish it and give Monmouth a 14-0 lead midway through the first quarter. "We wanted to come up here and be the more physical team, the more energized team," Gallo said. "To be able to run the ball into the wind and find some throws with the wind at our back. And I think just the o-line and running backs, we set the tone." The Hawks were also the beneficiaries of several New Hampshire lapses that combined with difficult windy conditions to put the Wildcats in an early hole. There were several drops, offset by many overthrows, as the UNH offense couldn't get anything going in the first half. To further exasperate the situation for the home team, swirling winds undermined any attempts by either team to punt. That was less of an issue for Monmouth, who started in opposing territory on four of their first six drives and each of those resulted in a touchdown. Monmouth seized on New Hampshire's struggles and capitalized on every opportunity. The strong run game set up a play action pass from quarterback Frankie Weaver to Tra Neal for 35-yard touchdown to extend the lead to 21-0 after the first quarter. Weaver finished the day 16-for-25 for 195 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions, while Neal had a team-high 82 receiving yards on five catches. After the offense stalled slightly on the two next possessions, the Hawks finished the half strong by going back to the run game. The wide-open running lanes were cleared by upperclassmen that had experienced the years of struggles against New Hampshire, like senior center Kevin Shriner, guard Michael Petito, and tight end Shane Garrett, all of whom got to enjoy the catharsis of a physically-dominating effort upfront. For Garrett, that effort was appropriately rewarded with a play action touchdown pass from Weaver to close out the first half with a 28-0 lead. It was the first career touchdown reception for the redshirt junior from Ocean Township. "He's a program kid. He works his butt off. He's everything you want in a player," Gallo "Shore kid, great family, son of a coach. He comes to work every day and he does all the dirty work. And when we throw it to him, he's gonna catch it." New Hampshire's offensive challenges were exacerbated by the Monmouth defense, and the Wildcats decided to make quarterback change after starter Brooks Bentley was just 3-for-11 for 29 yards at halftime. That did appear to slightly spark the Wildcats momentarily, as they opened the second half by forcing a three-and-out and then running back Myles Thomason, a former Seton Hall Prep standout, authored a two-play drive with 44 rushing yards and a touchdown. But that would be the only glimmer of hope for New Hampshire. The Hawks answered with a nine-play, 75-yard drive that culminated with a 27-yard touchdown by Smith. The Hawks carried a 35-7 lead until the final five minutes, when both teams added late points with the game already decided. Those seven points allowed until garbage time are strong testament to the Monmouth defense, which took advantage of the New Hampshire mistakes and created plenty of negative plays on their own. Ryan Russo had a crucial forced fumble that set up the Hawks' touchdown before halftime. Mounir Keshen and JJ Lewis both contributed sacks, an impressive showing for two front four players that are also reliable run defenders. And a third down pressure by Jahide Lesaine resulted in an interception by Jaeden Jones in the third quarter. The win is quite the milestone for the Hawks. It's obviously always a breakthrough to get a first-ever win against a conference opponent, but it was also encouraging that there was no lag in the team's performance coming out of the bye week. Furthermore, it was their first game since Monmouth rejoined the FCS top 25 two weeks ago. They'll likely see another rankings bump after the decisive victory. More importantly, the Hawks continue to sit atop the CAA standings as the only 4-0 team in conference play. Monmouth got a big boost from Albany on Saturday, as the Great Danes knocked off rival Stony Brook 48-31. The Seawolves were the only other remaining unbeaten in the CAA that Monmouth doesn't play this season, and their loss means the Hawks control their own destiny to a conference title. No. 18 Campbell (6-1, 3-0) and Bryant (5-2, 3-0) are the other remaining unbeaten teams in league play. Monmouth will be on the road next Saturday against 1-6 Hampton and will need to not look past that game even as a Halloween showdown at home against Bryant looms. "Focus on what matters, and that's playing your best football," Gallo said. "Was it our best football? No. We can play better. We played relatively well, but there's room for improvement. And now we focus on the next one at Hampton and we're gonna bring the same mentality. It's a road game in the CAA. It's their homecoming. It's a great opportunity for us and a great challenge. The rankings don't matter to me, it's more about how we play." Obviously a recurring theme for the Hawks is one-week seasons and that will need to continue to avoid any let downs before the key matchup against Bryant in two weeks. But for this week's season, finally beating New Hampshire carried a bit more weight and thusly, a bit more cathartic relief. "We were aware that we hadn't beaten them, but it was about this team, this year, this game," Gallo said. "We came out and really got after it, which was great to see. And it's great for our alumni, it's great for our university, it's great for our fans. It's a good program win." With the wild winds limiting the options in the passing game to create offensive balance, the Hawks became more dynamic in the run game with a wide variety of designs and formations to keep the New Hampshire defense off-balance. The periphery movement and unique formations were clever disguises for a rushing attack that also deployed several counter punches in addition to straightforward dominance at the line of scrimmage. The first two touchdowns epitomized what worked so well for the Monmouth offense on Saturday. On the first score, Nazir Treadwell came out in a variation of the usual goal line wildcat formation, which was tweaked to sub out the quarterback for an extra blocker. Tra Neal motioned in for a chip on the left side, creating enough space for G/H power (guard and h-back pulling) to clear the way to the end zone. The second score was a more conventional variation of a similar concept. This time the Hawks came out in a pistol unbalanced formation and motioned Gavin Nelson to be the chip blocker and again they pulled the left guard Collin Goetter on power. But instead of a second puller, the "H" element was in insert block from tight end Marcus Middleton, paving the way for Kenny Smith on the 6-yard touchdown. In the second quarter, the Hawks used an even bolder design to spark an explosive run play. Monmouth initially came out in an ace set with two slot receivers to the left, motioned tight end to the right for a twins set, and then pulled center Kevin Shriner and guard Reed Collins on a what appeared to be a buck sweep to the short side of the field. The look allowed Smith to turn the corner for a 33-yard gain. The play actions looks were more conventional, although the last touchdown of the first half to Shane Garrett was interesting. Garrett lined up in the slot and then motioned across to give the appearance of split zone, but he raced to the flat in what appeared to be a lower red zone run-pass option for Frankie Weaver as opposed to straight play action. And the third layer to the various designs helped put the game out of reach. The Hawks got their first touchdown of the second half on a really fascinating run design. The Hawks came out with trips to the left and Smith also aligned to the left of Weaver, a de facto quads set to the short side of the field. The lone receiver to the right, Keshawn Mister, moved backwards across the formation to give a reverse look, which cleared the space for the play's true intent: a G/H sweep with Goetter and Middleton pulling to clear the way for Smith's 27-yard touchdown. What is very cool about that play is that it is a Wing-T concept in principle with the misdirection, but executed out of a traditional spread formation. With an additional bye week to prepare and the motivation to beat New Hampshire for the first time, the Hawks brought out some of their best run designs in the win. There were some intriguing defensive fronts, particularly on third down, that the Monmouth defense used to stifle a New Hampshire offense that also shot itself in the foot. But instead of focusing on the X's and the O's, it's time to highlight some Jimmys and Joes that are emerging for the Hawks. JJ Lewis has to be at the top of the list. The senior joined Monmouth last year as a transfer from D-II Findlay, and he has come into his own this fall. In addition to his sack, he recovered Russo's first fumble that led to the key score before halftime. He is second on the team with three sacks and also has two pass break ups. His ability to be a disruptive presence on the interior is a huge boost for the front four as a whole, as the interior is usually shaped by stalwart run defenders. Lewis has shown the ability to do both. Complimenting him on the edge is Mounir Keshen, who continues his ascent as a premier defender, and Hunter Watson. So much of Monmouth's sack production last year was on third down in clear passing situations, but Watson and Keshen have emerged as premier rushers on early downs in addition to being stout against the run. Keshen leads the team with 3.5 sacks while Watson also has three. The growth of the trio of Watson, Keshen and Lewis has the potential to be a game-changer for the Hawks down the stretch. With limited angles on the broadcast of a road game, it's challenging to assess exactly what's happening in the secondary. The Hawks continue to use a deep rotation of players with varying results, as positive flashes can also be offset by maddening lapses. But the bright spot continues to be the safeties. Jaeden Jones is of course a star, but Donovan Fey had several excellent moments against UNH. He seemed to recognize a potential coverage breakdown in pre-snap, and recovered to the seam for a key pass breakup in the first half. He can be a nightmare for opposing receivers, delivering punishing hits while attacking the catch point to separate his man from the ball. Aside from some late coverage lapses and two runs by Myles Thomason that went for 44 yards and a score, this was a lights-out performance from the Monmouth defense. The Hawks will look to build on it next week against Hampton. We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. title: College football: No. 23 Monmouth rides ground game past UNH, 42-21 - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — The University of New Hampshire football team dropped a 42-21 decision to No. 23 Monmouth on Saturday, Oct. 17 at Wildcat Stadium. Monmouth rushed for 301 yards and scored six touchdowns to improve to 5-2 overall and 4-0 in conference play. New Hampshire dropped to 2-6 overall and 1-4 in the CAA. Sophomore linebacker Trevor Barry led the Wildcats defensively with a career-high 20 tackles, including 12 solo stops. Grad student safety Jackson Stone added a career-best 16 tackles and surpassed the 100-career tackle mark, while sophomore safety Cohen Cook made 12 tackles. Sophomore linebacker Matthew Sopp also registered a personal-best 10 tackles. Monmouth's rushing attack controlled the game, led by Kenny Smith Jr., who ran 27 times for 175 yards and two touchdowns. Elijah Jennings added 126 yards and a touchdown on 28 carries. Quarterback Frankie Weaver completed 16 of 25 passes for 195 yards and two touchdowns. The Wildcats received offensive contributions from several players. Grad student running back Myles Thomason rushed for 70 yards on seven carries, and scored on an 11-yard touchdown run. Junior wide receiver Ty Carlson led New Hampshire's receiving corps with 62 yards, including a 41-yard touchdown reception. Sophomore quarterback Tommy McLeish entered in the second half and sparked the offense, completing 13 of 19 passes for 178 yards while directing three touchdown drives. The Wildcats return to action Oct. 24 when they travel to Merrimack. New Hampshire's next home game is Nov. 7 against Rhode Island. We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. title: David Ismail ends scoring drought, leads Vermont soccer to comeback win over UNH - Burlington Free Press
content: David Ismail ended a two-month scoring drought and Vermont soccer prolonged a yearslong home unbeaten streak typical Catamount fashion: A second-half comeback with a late-regulation winner. Ismail, who scored for the first time since Aug. 23 with a first-half penalty strike, blasted in the go-ahead goal in the 84th minute, capping Vermont's rally for a 3-2 victory over New Hampshire in front of 2,197 at windy Virtue Field on Saturday, Oct. 17. No. 16 Vermont (9-1-3, 3-0-1), which trailed 2-1 at the break, also extended its regular-season home unbeaten run to 27 consecutive games (19-0-8), a streak that started on Oct. 27, 2023. "Love the guys’ response.  What a great second-half attitude and what a way to turn the tide … and never give up," said Vermont first-year head coach Adrian Dubois, who is an UNH alum. "That is what Vermont football is. When you do that, good things are going to happen." After Vermont was rewarded a PK following an officials' video review, Ismail converted from the spot in the 10th minute for a 1-0 lead. But the Catamounts, challenged by the windy conditions on defense, conceded a pair of goals in the 24th and 32nd minute, respectively. On the first UNH goal, Laurin Preuss supplied a pretty flick via Ryo Myata's corner kick that slipped under the bar to level the game. Then David Dravila rolled a shot past Vermont goalie Niklas Herceg (four saves), a goal that was initially ruled offside before another review overturned the call. In the second half, Ismail had two door-step chances with headers — the first smacked off the cross bar, the second UNH goalie Aaron Choi (five saves) snatched above his head. But in the 70th minute, the Catamounts found the equalizer via Philipp Schmidtke's fifth goal of 2026. A failed UNH clearance in the box fell to Schmidtke, who uncorked a lefty blast inside the left post. On the winner, Ismail uncorked a lefty rocket into the back of the net with authority for the 84th-minute winner, also his fifth goal this fall. "He’s a top player. He’s going to find a way. I’m just happy for him because he’s the hardest worker on the team," Dubois said of Ismail. "That’s going to give him a boost of energy and we need our best guys playing well right now. He had a really good game overall." Vermont travels to Albany for its next game on Saturday, Oct. 24. Contact Alex Abrami at aabrami@freepressmedia.com. title: Wrong-way crash on I-91 in North Haven leaves 1 dead, several injured - WFSB
content:
NORTH HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - A multi-vehicle crash caused by a wrong-way driver on I-91 southbound in North Haven left one person dead on Friday night. Troopers were called to the area of I-91 south near Exit 9 at around 11:43 p.m. after reports of a wrong-way driver where the vehicle was then involved in a multi-vehicle crash, according to state police. EMS and fire department personnel also responded to the scene, and the Connecticut Department of Transportation assisted with road closures. A man driving a Honda Accord was heading southbound on I-91 in the left lane while a man driving a pick up truck was traveling the wrong-way and struck his car in a head-on collision. The man who’s vehicle was struck then entered the left-center lane, where it was struck by another vehicle, a Jeep. The man then entered the right lane and right shoulder, where it was struck by a GMC SUV, state police said. State Police have identified the driver of the Honda Accord that was struck as 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea from Stony Point, New York. The University of New Haven confirmed that he was a criminal justice major with a concentration in police science at the school. He interned last summer with the New York City Police Department, where he hoped to start his career as a police officer after commencement. He was also a senior captain of the university’s club hockey team. O’Shea suffered fatal injuries in the crash and died on scene. The driver of the GMC SUV was transported to a nearby hospital with serious injuries. Also, the driver and the front passenger who were in the Jeep were suffered minor injuries and were transported to a local hospital as well as the driver of the GMC. The State Police Collision Analysis and Reconstruction Squad responded to the scene and is assisting with the investigation. State Police said this remains under active investigation. title: Kidder Lecture and LGBTQ+ Resource Fair - University of New Hampshire
content: This annual event highlights issues related to LGBTQIA+ identities and inclusion. The lecture brings prominent speakers, scholars, and advocates to campus to engage the community in meaningful conversations about sexual orientation, gender identity, and belonging. The event serves as an opportunity for the members of the UNH Community to learn, reflect, and deepen their understanding of diverse experiences. The Kidder Lecture is followed by the LGBTQ+ Resource Fair. It brings together various on-campus departments and community-based organizations to highlight resources for members of the LGBTQ+ Members of the UNH Community and allies. The Kidder Lecture is supported by the Kidder Fund, established by William “Bill” Kidder, a UNH alumnus and former associate dean of students. The fund supports educational initiatives, awards, and programming that promote awareness and inclusion for individuals of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. As a signature campus event, the Kidder Lecture and LGBTQ+ Resource Fair reflects UNH’s ongoing commitment to fostering an inclusive and welcoming community for all. For questions and additional information, please contact Ramonda "Monda" Kindle at Ramonda.Kindle@unh.edu Register Today for the 2026 Kidder Lecture and LGBTQ+ Resource Fair! Click Here for the 2026 Kidder Lecture Registration Form Please fill out the Registration Form no later than 11:59pm on October 19, 2026 in order to attend the event in-person. Virtual registrants will be accepted until Thursday, October 22, 2026 We are excited to announce Queerlective Founder and Executive Director Randall Nielsen as the keynote speaker for the 2026 Kidder Lecture. Date: Monday, October 26, 2026Time: 12:00 pm - 1:30 pm Location: Strafford Room, Memorial Union Building (MUB), Durham Campus The Resource Fair will immediately follow the Kidder Lecture from 1:30 pm - 5:00 pm. Lunch will be served for in-person Kidder Lecture guests Registration is on a first-come, first-served basis until the event is at capacity This event is open to all UNH undergraduate, graduate, and professional students, faculty, staff, administrators, and alumni 2026-2027 Chair: Ramonda Kindle, Aulbani J. Beauregard Center for Equity, Justice, and Freedom Christina Juris, Undergraduate Student Senate DEI Council Chair Sam Crawford, Graduate Student Senate Representative Kelsey Boucher, Clinical Associate Professor, School of Social Work Deborah Briand, Academic Department Coordinator, College of Liberal Arts Michelle Bronner, Deputy Director and Senior Woman Administrator, Athletics Lu Butterfield-Ferrell, Program Manager, New Hampshire Listens Holly Cashman, Professor, Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture Evan England, Assistant Director, Center for Social Policy in Practice Amanda Harvey, Administrative Coordinator, UNH Office for Faculty Excellence Sarah Leonard, Director of Child Study and Development Center, Human Development and Family Studies Elena Long, Associate Professor, College of Engineering and Physical Sciences Ally Twitchell, Coordinator for Student Involvement and Student Success, Manchester Campus Kai Uchida, Assistant Professor/University Archivist, Dimond Library Erica Vazza, Assistant Director of Engagement and Prevention, The SHARPP Center Linds Jakows discussed the importance of taking action for LGBTQIA+ Thriving: In and Outside of the Political System. UNH Alumnae Brady Barre discussed New Hampshire Outright and the importance of mutual aid. Tona Brown discussed her book, Tonacity: The Tona Brown Story. The event included an interview conducted by a UNH student, a Q&A, and a book signing opportunity. Sarah Leonard, UNH Early Childhood Teacher, UNH Child Study & Development Center Joelle Ryan, UNH Faculty, UNH Department of Women’s & Gender Studies Noele Lee, Lecturer, Decision Sciences, Paul College Laquincy (Lionel) Loveless, Officially Knotted Bowties, Portsmouth Frederic Mason, Executive Director, Large Cap Sector Specialist, J.P. Morgan Asset Management Trans UNH and UNH Stonewall Grads hosted a virtual film screening of Coded Black with a group discussion of the film.  Participants we encouraged to bring their dinner to the screening and shared their thoughts on the themes raised in the film and considered their responsibilities to addressing the issues highlighted. Simmons College Professor Gary Bailey explored the climate of amplification of homophobia, sexism, racism, and other biases. Participants examined the way we assign “outcast” status to people/groups within our communities and ways some people may unintentionally participate in the process even though they reject the beliefs. Robyn Ochs discussed building acceptance and respect for individual choice and political & legal legitimization for people’s gender, sexual and romantic identities.  The discussion concluded with advocating for the rights of people to live safely, openly and with full access and opportunity. Mara Keisling discussed the significance of advocating for the “T” in our LGBTQIA+ community at UNH and beyond and how to create a community where transphobia and microaggressions are eliminated. Erin E. Buzuvis discussed policies that the NCAA and various sport organizations adopted for the purpose of determining the eligibility of transgender athletics to compete according to their gender identities and advocated for policies that are as inclusive as possible under the circumstances particular to those organizations. The College of Liberal Arts hosted Roma Baran, and Anne Philbin to discuss their experiences at UNH and what each took away from their experiences that helped define where they are today. In an evening chat, Dr. Darrow shared his lived experiences as the former Chief of Behavioral and Prevention Research Branch, Division of STD/HIV Prevention at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and a consultant for World Health Organization, the European Union, and the Global Program on AIDS. Arbutus Biopharma (ABUS) stock rose 6% on Thursday after the company announced new international patent lawsuits, receipt of a large settlement payment from Moderna and plans to return up to $230 million to shareholders. The stock is now on track for its best day since May 2026 after five consecutive days of trading in the red. On July 8, Arbutus received around $178 million from Moderna, the company said. This represents its share of the payment under the March 2026 global settlement that resolved all patent litigation over Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. In March, Arbutus and its partner Genevant Sciences, a unit of Roivant Sciences (ROIV), reached a global settlement with Moderna worth up to $2.25 billion to resolve a long-running dispute over technology used in Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. Under the agreement, Moderna is required to make a $950 million upfront payment to both parties, and the payout on July 8 was part of it. The remaining will be paid to Genevant under the settlement agreement. The Moderna patent litigation centered on whether Moderna had used Arbutus’s patented technology without permission in its COVID-19 vaccine. At its core, the dispute was over lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the tiny fat particles that protect and deliver mRNA into human cells. Without effective LNPs, mRNA vaccines like Moderna’s covid vaccine Spikevax would not work well. Arbutus had developed and patented specific LNP formulations years before the pandemic. Arbutus now expects a dividend from Roivant in the third quarter, owing to its stake in the Genevant parent. Arbutus said it expects to begin returning up to about $230 million to shareholders through share repurchases starting in the third quarter. The buybacks may take the form of a tender offer, open-market purchases, or other methods and will follow receipt of the expected Genevant dividend. However, there is no assurance of the share repurchase activity, the company noted. Following the successful payout from Moderna, Arbutus and Genevant also filed three lawsuits against Pfizer Inc., BioNTech SE and certain of their affiliates to enforce patents covering lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology used in their mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. Cases were lodged in Canada’s Federal Court and two proceedings at the Unified Patent Court in Europe. The company seeks damages and injunctions against Pfizer/BioNTech’s vaccines and any future infringing products. These actions expand an ongoing U.S. patent case in New Jersey. For years, the race to build better artificial intelligence centered on making models bigger, feeding them more data, and expanding the amount of information they could process at once. Now, a fresh frontier is emerging as researchers increasingly explore smarter memory management as another way to build more capable AI systems. Two academic papers published this month, AutoMem and SelfMem, argue that memory shouldn't be a rigid feature engineered by developers using static rules. Instead, they propose that AI systems can learn to manage their own memories. They take different approaches: AutoMem trains AI to manage an external memory system, while SelfMem lets agents refine their own memory strategies through feedback, and both report substantial gains on long-horizon benchmarks. Imagine working with an AI coding assistant on a project for months. Instead of repeatedly reminding it about your project's architecture and coding style, a smarter memory system could retain the decisions that matter while discarding obsolete information. Researchers believe that this kind of selective memory will become increasingly important as AI agents take on longer-running tasks. One way developers have tried to build more capable chatbots is by expanding their context windows, which are the immediate digital scratchpad an AI considers during a conversation. While larger context windows let models process more information, they also increase computational costs and don't necessarily help AI distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. The papers instead explore an alternative approach based on active memory curation. In AutoMem, Stanford University researchers introduced a memory manager that decides when to create, update, search, and delete records, allowing the AI to maintain a compact memory instead of continuously accumulating information. Tested on grueling, complex video games like NetHack and Crafter, this memory-management approach slashed the agent's memory growth rate by 95% and doubled its task performance, allowing a 32-billion-parameter open-weight model to perform competitively with frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking on the evaluated long-horizon benchmarks. SelfMem takes a completely parameter-free approach. Instead of editing model weights, it gives the AI a dedicated workspace and tools to inspect an unchangeable transcript store. It allows the agent to inspect, write, review, and revise its own memory, outperforming traditional retrieval pipelines by more than 40% on the BEAM benchmark while using only a fraction of the computational cost. The push for smarter memory comes as AI companies shift from one-off chatbots to autonomous agents designed to work over days or weeks. Whether writing software, tracking supply chains, or managing research projects, these systems must retain relevant information while discarding details that no longer matter. That is where autonomous memory management changes the equation. Instead of forcing a user to repeatedly copy-paste instructions, an agent equipped with an optimized memory workflow seamlessly recalls structural boundaries, tracks cumulative progress, and discards transient data that is no longer relevant. Better memory could also reduce the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same information, a potential advantage as AI companies look to deploy agents more efficiently at scale. Over the past year, leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic have introduced basic memory features, allowing consumer chatbots to retain user preferences and custom instructions across distinct chat sessions. Today's commercial memory features generally rely on predefined mechanisms for deciding what information is retained. AutoMem and SelfMem instead point toward AI systems capable of independently evaluating and regulating their own memories. As tech companies race to build AI systems capable of executing truly long-horizon work, the findings suggest memory management may become an increasingly important complement to larger models. Future AI systems may be judged not only by how much they know, but also by how effectively they decide what information is worth keeping. Lucid Motors (LCID) shares rose for a second straight day on Thursday after the electric vehicle maker forcefully rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, rebounding from a brutal selloff earlier in the week. The stock traded 12% higher at the time of writing and is on track to clock its best week since July 2025, thanks to a 29% jump on Wednesday, if gains hold. The stock’s dramatic rise and fall started after an Electric-Vehicles.com report on Tuesday said that restructuring adviser AlixPartners has outlined scenarios to the company’s board, including taking the company private or seeking Chapter 11 protection. The stock fell as much as 50% on the news, but pared gains after the company refuted the report as “completely false.” “The company has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year, as recently published in its last quarterly filings, and it has not formed any special Board committee to explore the scenarios reported today,” Lucid said in a statement to Stocktwits. It also added that AlixPartners is only assisting the company to improve operational performance and did not advise Lucid on a take-private transaction or bankruptcy. They further didn't suggest either option to the company management or board, it added. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, also said in a post on LinkedIn that the claims circulated were “far from the facts” and that he looks forward to providing a full update on its quarterly earnings call on August 4. Lucid, majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), has faced significant headwinds as an electric vehicle maker. Earlier this month, the company reported second-quarter production of 4,774 vehicles and deliveries of 3,953 units— marking a modest year-over-year increase but short of analyst expectations amid slower-than-hoped demand for the new Gravity SUV. The results coincided with a sweeping leadership overhaul under CEO Silvio Napoli, who assumed the role in June. Napoli replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock, appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. In the first quarter, it posted revenue of $282.5 million, up 20% year-over-year, but recorded a net loss of approximately $1.03 billion. The company has relied heavily on its majority shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, for support. It raised about $1.05 billion in April, including $550 million in preferred stock from PIF, $200 million from Uber, and a public offering, and drew an additional $800 million from an existing delayed-draw term loan facility in early July.
